propositions.text: Upholding rights by fostering trial fairness and safeguarding liberty is central to criminal justice.
propositions.quote: Upholding the rights of Canadian citizens by fostering trial fairness and safeguarding liberty interests is central to the criminal justice process.

propositions.text: Access to courts is central to democracy and grounded in freedom of expression.
propositions.quote: At the same time, access to the courts is central to a democratic society; it is a means to protect against arbitrary state action. Access to the courts is grounded in freedom of expression.

propositions.text: Trial fairness and liberty interests must be reconciled with freedom of expression.
propositions.quote: Trial fairness and liberty interests must not clash with freedom of expression. They can be reconciled.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that trial fairness, liberty, and freedom of expression must be reconciled in criminal justice and democracy.

propositions.text: Media organizations argue s. 517 unjustifiably violates freedom of expression under the Charter.
propositions.quote: A number of media organizations are urging this Court to find that s. 517 of the Criminal Code... unjustifiably violates the freedom of expression guaranteed by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

propositions.text: Section 517 mandates a publication ban on bail hearing evidence and reasons if requested by accused or prosecutor.
propositions.quote: Under this provision, a justice... shall... make an order directing that the evidence taken... shall not be published...

propositions.text: There is no question s. 517 limits freedom of expression.
propositions.quote: There is no question that this order limits freedom of expression.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the limit on expression is justified in a free and democratic society.
propositions.quote: The issue is whether that limit can be justified in a free and democratic society.

propositions.text: The mandatory publication ban is justified; appeals dismissed or allowed as specified.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I conclude that the statutory mandatory publication ban is justified... I would dismiss the appeal and allow the cross-appeal in the Ontario case and dismiss the appeal in the Alberta case.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue s. 517 violates expression rights; court finds the mandatory ban justified and disposes appeals accordingly.

propositions.text: Context is key to understanding limits on Charter rights, per Thomson Newspapers and Oakes test.
propositions.quote: Context is the key to understanding the scope and impact of a limit on a Charter right... requires a court to establish the objective of the impugned provision...

propositions.text: Will consider historical and legislative context, limits on expression, and justification under Oakes test.
propositions.quote: To properly assess the challenge... it will be necessary to consider the historical and legislative context... then review the limits on freedom of expression... before discussing justification under the Oakes framework.

propositions.text: Appellants argue facts show need to promote openness in interim release provisions.
propositions.quote: The appellants argued these appeals on the basis of two different sets of facts that... demonstrate the need to promote openness...

propositions.text: Will set out facts of the two cases first.
propositions.quote: I will thus begin by briefly setting out the facts in these two cases.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains context and Oakes test framework, will review facts and legislative background before analysis.

propositions.text: Michael White charged with murder in Alberta, granted bail with s. 517 publication ban ordered.
propositions.quote: Michael White was charged with the murder of his wife in Alberta. He was granted bail... and a publication ban was ordered pursuant to s. 517 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Appellants say White's release provoked public outrage and ban's constitutionality was challenged successfully in Court of Queen's Bench.
propositions.quote: According to the appellants, Mr. White’s release provoked public outrage. The constitutionality of the ban was then challenged successfully in the Court of Queen’s Bench...

propositions.text: Brooker J. found ban's objective was to protect fair trial but no rational connection or minimal impairment found.
propositions.quote: Brooker J. found that the legislative objective underlying the ban was to protect the right of the accused to a fair trial... reason and logic alone were insufficient to establish a rational connection... means also failed to meet the minimal impairment test.

paragraphs.summary: In Alberta case, bail granted with publication ban; lower court found ban lacked rational connection and minimal impairment.

propositions.text: Alberta Court of Appeal reversed Brooker J., found ban merely defers publication and benefits outweigh harms.
propositions.quote: The Alberta Court of Appeal reversed Brooker J.’s decision... concluded that a s. 517 ban merely defers publication and... benefits outweighed the deleterious effects.

paragraphs.summary: Alberta Court of Appeal reversed lower court, upholding s. 517 ban as justified and beneficial.

propositions.text: In Ontario case, 17 charged with terrorism offences attracting massive media attention.
propositions.quote: On June 2, 2006, twelve adults and five young persons were charged with various terrorism-related offences... The arrests attracted massive media attention...

propositions.text: One accused applied for publication ban; others opposed it.
propositions.quote: One of the accused applied for a publication ban, while some of the others opposed it.

paragraphs.summary: Ontario case involved terrorism charges with media attention; one accused sought publication ban, others opposed.

propositions.text: Justice of the Peace Currie ordered ban; appellants moved to quash it but application dismissed by Durno J.
propositions.quote: On June 12, 2006, Justice of the Peace Currie ordered a ban. The appellants moved to quash the order. Durno J.... dismissed their application...

propositions.text: Durno J. held s. 517 ban applies to all co-accused if one seeks it.
propositions.quote: Durno J.... holding that if one accused seeks a ban under s. 517, the order applies to all his or her co-accused.

propositions.text: Some accused released pending trial, others remained in custody; constitutionality challenged.
propositions.quote: Some of the accused were released pending their trial, while others remained in custody. The appellants and two of the accused challenged the constitutionality of s. 517.

propositions.text: Durno J. found bound by precedent and held s. 517 does not infringe Charter.
propositions.quote: Durno J.... held that s. 517 does not infringe the Charter.

paragraphs.summary: Ontario lower courts upheld s. 517 ban applying to all co-accused; constitutionality challenge dismissed based on precedent.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal majority found s. 517 overbroad but objective pressing and substantial and rationally connected.
propositions.quote: Feldman J.A.... found that s. 517 was overbroad... objective... was pressing and substantial and that the ban was rationally connected to the objective.

propositions.text: Provision failed minimal impairment test as it applied to all charges regardless of trial mode.
propositions.quote: She concluded that... the provision did not meet the minimal impairment test, because it applied to bail hearings in respect of all charges regardless of the mode of trial.

propositions.text: Feldman J.A. read down s. 517 to exclude non-jury trial cases from ban.
propositions.quote: As a remedy, Feldman J.A. read s. 517 down to exclude from the ban any cases in which the charges would not be tried by a jury.

propositions.text: Dissent would have declared mandatory ban invalid for failing proportionality test.
propositions.quote: Rosenberg J.A., dissenting... would have declared the part of s. 517 relating to the mandatory ban to be invalid on the basis that it did not meet the requirement of proportionality...

propositions.text: Appellants ask Court to adopt dissent's view; respondents cross-appeal arguing provision is valid.
propositions.quote: The appellants ask this Court to adopt the view of the dissent, while the respondents cross-appeal, arguing that the provision is valid.

paragraphs.summary: Ontario Court of Appeal majority found s. 517 overbroad but partially valid; dissent would invalidate; parties contest these views.

propositions.text: Bail developed in English law to avoid jail deaths, initially focused on ensuring accused's attendance at trial.
propositions.quote: Bail was developed in early English law not as a means to further the liberty interest of the accused but as a response to the deplorable conditions of jails...

propositions.text: In Canada, attendance at trial was predominant bail consideration, later expanded to public protection.
propositions.quote: In Canada, too, the likelihood of attendance at trial was initially the predominant consideration. However, additional factors subsequently came to be developed, such as the need to protect the public from repeat offenders.

propositions.text: Bail process remained informal and discretionary until mid-20th century (Trotter).
propositions.quote: The process for granting bail remained quite informal and discretionary until the middle of the 20th century (G. T. Trotter, The Law of Bail in Canada (2nd ed. 1999), at pp. 3-9).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains bail's historical development from English law focusing on attendance to broader public protection in Canada.

propositions.text: 1965 Friedland study found many detained unnecessarily and linked pre-trial detention to conviction and sentences.
propositions.quote: Disturbing data then emerged from an empirical study by Prof. Martin Friedland... observed that the existing procedures resulted in the detention of many individuals whose attendance could have been secured by less restrictive means... noted a relationship between pre‑trial detention, conviction and custodial sentences.

propositions.text: Study prompted re-examination of bail rules by Ontario Royal Commission and Canadian Committee on Corrections.
propositions.quote: This study prompted a re-examination of the rules on bail by the Ontario Royal Commission... and by the Canadian Committee on Corrections...

paragraphs.summary: Friedland's 1965 study revealed unnecessary detention and links to convictions, prompting bail rule reforms.

propositions.text: Ouimet Report found other factors relevant to interim release beyond attendance at trial.
propositions.quote: The authors of the Ouimet Report found that considerations other than ensuring the attendance of the accused at trial were relevant to the decision whether to order interim release.

propositions.text: Report emphasized minimal interference with freedom, negative impacts of pre-trial detention, and presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: They stated... that '[t]he basic purposes of the criminal law should be carried out with no more interference with the freedom of individuals than is necessary'... pre-trial incarceration could lead to loss of employment... release intended to ensure individuals were not punished while presumed innocent.

propositions.text: Pre-trial custody could cause stigma and affect corrective measures if convicted.
propositions.quote: They accepted that incarceration could result in a permanent stigma... how an accused was treated between arraignment and trial had an impact on the corrective measures...

propositions.text: From human rights perspective, accused should not be incarcerated pre-trial unless society protection requires it.
propositions.quote: From a human rights perspective, the authors considered it clear that an accused should not be incarcerated while awaiting trial unless the protection of society made it necessary to do so.

paragraphs.summary: Ouimet Report highlighted minimal interference, harms of pre-trial detention, and human rights basis for release unless necessary.

propositions.text: Ouimet Report recommended police release powers, prosecution onus, early bail hearings, publication bans, and accused informed of ban rights.
propositions.quote: The authors of the Ouimet Report made a number of recommendations, including that police officers be allowed to release accused persons... onus be placed on the prosecution... provision for a publication ban... justice be required to inform the accused of the right to a ban.

propositions.text: Report emphasized release as rule and custody as exception with limited grounds for refusal.
propositions.quote: One of the most important features... was that limited grounds for refusing interim release were identified. Under reformed rules... release should be the rule and custody the exception.

paragraphs.summary: Ouimet Report recommended reforms including publication bans and presumption of release over custody with limited refusal grounds.

propositions.text: Ouimet Report's recommendations led to Criminal Code amendments requiring prompt justice appearance, release unless Crown shows cause, and mandatory publication bans if requested.
propositions.quote: As can be seen from the subsequent amendments to the Criminal Code... the government embraced most of the Report’s recommendations... mandatory publication ban would have to be ordered if requested by the accused.

propositions.text: Minister of Justice promoted reforms as protecting individual rights and making first contact less abrasive.
propositions.quote: John Turner, the then Minister of Justice, declared... 'This bill is directed at making that first contact between citizens and the criminal judicial process less abrasive.'

paragraphs.summary: Criminal Code amendments implemented Ouimet Report reforms, including mandatory publication bans, promoted as protecting rights.

propositions.text: Interim release reforms predated Charter but foreshadowed rights consciousness; bail now constitutionally protected under s. 11(e).
propositions.quote: The reform of the rules governing interim release was implemented long before the Charter but foreshadowed the period of consciousness of individual rights... constitutional right to bail is... recognized in s. 11 (e) of the Charter.

propositions.text: Bail protection is procedural and substantive; bail process linked to right to bail.
propositions.quote: The protection is both procedural and substantive... the bail process is inextricably linked to the right to bail itself.

paragraphs.summary: Interim release reforms anticipated Charter rights; bail is now a constitutional right with procedural and substantive protections.

propositions.text: Openness permits public access and discussion of courts; publication bans infringe expression (Canadian Broadcasting Corp. v. New Brunswick).
propositions.quote: As La Forest J. stated in Canadian Broadcasting Corp. v. New Brunswick... '[o]penness permits public access to information about the courts...'.

propositions.text: Publication bans infringe expression but must be balanced with accused's rights; clash model rejected (Dagenais).
propositions.quote: A publication ban therefore infringes freedom of expression. However, it should not be concluded that there is a conflict... The 'clash model' was rejected in Dagenais... the Court must engage in a balancing exercise...

propositions.text: Dagenais test applies beyond trial fairness to proper administration of justice (New Brunswick, Mentuck).
propositions.quote: In New Brunswick... La Forest J.... recognized that the interest of the proper administration of justice could justify banning the press... In R. v. Mentuck... the Court applied the balancing test to another aspect of the proper administration of justice.

propositions.text: Publication bans can serve broad objectives beyond fair trial rights (Mentuck).
propositions.quote: Iacobucci J. stressed... the rule can accommodate orders... in the interests of the administration of justice, which encompass more than fair trial rights.

paragraphs.summary: Prior cases establish publication bans infringe expression but require balancing with justice interests beyond fair trial rights.

propositions.text: Appellants argue s. 517 mandatory ban fails New Brunswick test due to lack of discretion and rational connection, and fails minimal impairment and proportionality.
propositions.quote: The appellants argue that the order provided for in s. 517 Cr. C. fails the New Brunswick test because it is mandatory... no rational connection... fails to meet the requirements of the minimal impairment and proportionality stages of the Oakes test.

propositions.text: Bans can be necessary; justification depends on context.
propositions.quote: As can be seen from the above cases, bans are sometimes necessary, and whether they are justified depends on the context.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue s. 517 mandatory ban fails constitutional tests; court notes bans can be necessary depending on context.

propositions.text: Appellants contend judicial discretion is a constitutional threshold for publication bans.
propositions.quote: The appellants accept that a limited publication ban may be valid... However, they contend that the existence of a judicial discretion amounts to a constitutional threshold.

propositions.text: Court rejects appellants' position that discretion is a constitutional threshold for limits on expression.
propositions.quote: In my view, their position does not reflect this Court’s approach to limits on freedom of expression.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue discretion is constitutional threshold; court rejects this position.

propositions.text: Existence of discretion is not determinative of validity of expression limits; mandatory bans can be constitutional.
propositions.quote: Whether a discretion exists is not determinative of the validity of a limit on freedom of expression...

propositions.text: Dagenais test applies to discretionary bans; mandatory bans require Charter challenge to legislation and Oakes analysis.
propositions.quote: As Lamer C.J. said in Dagenais... If legislation requires a judge to order a publication ban, then any objection... should be framed as a Charter challenge to the legislation itself... validity... determined by conducting an analysis based on the Oakes test.

propositions.text: Dagenais test not meant for all expression limits, only discretionary orders (Named Person, Vancouver Sun).
propositions.quote: As Bastarache J. stated in Named Person v. Vancouver Sun... the Dagenais test was not meant to apply to all limits on freedom of expression; rather, it was designed for and applies to discretionary orders.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains discretion is not determinative; mandatory bans require Charter and Oakes analysis, not Dagenais test.

propositions.text: Oakes test requires government to justify infringement by pressing objective, rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality.
propositions.quote: The various stages of the Oakes test are well known... government must justify its action by identifying a pressing and substantial objective... rational connection... minimal impairment... benefits outweigh deleterious effects.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Oakes test steps for justifying rights infringement.

propositions.text: Proper identification of objective is crucial for Oakes test analysis; overstating objective compromises analysis.
propositions.quote: Care must be taken not to overstate the objective... The objective relevant to the s. 1 analysis is the objective of the infringing measure... If the objective is stated too broadly, its importance may be exaggerated and the analysis compromised.

propositions.text: Proportionality examines if objective realization is commensurate with deleterious effect (Alberta v. Hutterian Brethren, Barak).
propositions.quote: McLachlin C.J.... endorsed... 'the test of proportionality (stricto sensu) examines whether the realization of this proper objective is commensurate with the deleterious effect upon the human right'...

propositions.text: All Oakes test steps premised on proper identification of impugned measure's objective.
propositions.quote: This suggests that all steps of the Oakes test are premised on a proper identification of the objective of the impugned measure.

paragraphs.summary: Court emphasizes importance of properly identifying objective for Oakes test and proportionality analysis.

propositions.text: The mandatory publication ban is part of a broad bail reform package by Parliament.
propositions.quote: The mandatory publication ban is but one of numerous interrelated measures adopted as part of a sweeping reform of the rules on bail.

propositions.text: To assess the ban's validity, its role within the broader bail reform must be understood.
propositions.quote: To assess the validity of the limit, it is necessary to understand the part the provision plays within the broader scheme of the reform.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the mandatory publication ban is part of bail reform and its validity must be assessed in that broader context.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal majority and dissent viewed the provision's objective as fostering trial fairness.
propositions.quote: In the Ontario Court of Appeal, both the majority and the dissent expressed the view that the objective of the provision is to foster trial fairness.

propositions.text: Trial fairness can mean more than preventing jury bias; it includes protecting accused's fundamental rights.
propositions.quote: Trial fairness has also been understood as encompassing all measures whose purpose it is to protect the fundamental rights of the accused

propositions.text: Cites cases and literature recognizing broader concept of trial fairness.
propositions.quote: see R. v. Burlingham, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 206, at para. 29; R. v. Stillman, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 607; and P. Mirfield, “The Early Jurisprudence of Judicial Disrepute”

propositions.text: Rosenberg J.A. dissent viewed trial fairness as including preventing resource diversion, delay, and ensuring expeditious bail hearings.
propositions.quote: The interest in a fair trial embraces not simply the narrow interest of preventing potential jurors from being influenced by prejudicial material...

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Ontario Court of Appeal saw the provision's objective as fostering broad trial fairness, including expeditious bail hearings and resource protection.

propositions.text: Bail reform followed Ouimet Report linking pre-trial custody to convictions and sentences.
propositions.quote: the bail reform was implemented following the Ouimet Report, according to which there appeared to be a correlation between pre-trial custody, conviction, and custodial sentences.

propositions.text: Ouimet Report emphasized first offender's initial justice system encounter is crucial and can have dire consequences.
propositions.quote: The Report’s authors stressed the fact that a first offender’s initial encounter with the justice system was crucial and could have dire consequences for the accused and his or her family.

propositions.text: Parliament's primary objectives include safeguarding fair trial rights and ensuring expeditious bail hearings.
propositions.quote: I would define Parliament’s objectives as (1) to safeguard the right to a fair trial; and (2) to ensure expeditious bail hearings.

propositions.text: These objectives aim to facilitate early release, mitigate stigma, and ensure impartial triers of fact.
propositions.quote: These objectives were to be achieved by establishing a process that facilitated early release of an accused in order to mitigate the harshness...

propositions.text: These objectives are pressing and grounded in Charter values.
propositions.quote: In view of the facts noted in the Ouimet Report, these objectives were undeniably pressing. Since they are solidly grounded in Charter values, they are also substantial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament's objectives from the Ouimet Report include fair trial rights and expeditious bail hearings, grounded in Charter values.

propositions.text: Appellants argue accepting expeditious bail hearings as an objective applies rejected 'shifting purpose' doctrine.
propositions.quote: The appellants argue that to accept ensuring expeditious bail hearings as an objective would be to apply the “shifting purpose” doctrine this Court explicitly rejected

propositions.text: Court explains expeditious bail hearings and trial fairness are inextricably linked, so no shifting purpose doctrine applies.
propositions.quote: the objectives of ensuring expeditious bail hearings and fostering trial fairness are inextricably linked, as the latter embraces the former.

propositions.text: This formulation is rooted in the Ouimet Report's analysis and does not violate the shifting purpose doctrine.
propositions.quote: this formulation of the objectives not only does not attract the prohibition against the shifting purpose doctrine, it is rooted in the Ouimet Report’s analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the objective is shifting purpose, but the court finds expeditious bail hearings and trial fairness linked, so no doctrine violation.

propositions.text: Next Oakes test stage: is there a rational connection between means and Parliament's objectives?
propositions.quote: At the next stage of the Oakes test, it must be asked whether there is a rational connection between the adopted means and Parliament’s objectives.

propositions.text: Government must show limit may further goal, not guarantee it; rational connection can be found by reason and logic.
propositions.quote: The government must show that it is reasonable to suppose that the limit may further the goal, not that it will do so

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting rational connection test.
propositions.quote: RJR‑MacDonald, at para. 158; Butler, at p. 503; R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, at pp. 768 and 776; Thomson Newspapers, at paras. 104-7.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Oakes test requires a rational connection between the limit and objectives, citing precedent.

propositions.text: Rational connection inquiry must consider the entire bail reform, not just the publication ban alone.
propositions.quote: since the mandatory publication ban is only one part of a whole, the enquiry cannot be limited to the ban itself.

paragraphs.summary: The court says rational connection must consider the whole bail reform, not just the ban.

propositions.text: Bail hearing mechanisms are closely linked and illustrate expeditious hearings and fair trial objectives.
propositions.quote: The mechanisms in place are closely linked. They illustrate the expeditious nature of the bail hearing and the ultimate objective of safeguarding the right to a fair trial.

propositions.text: Section 503(1)(a) requires prompt justice appearance within 24 hours of arrest.
propositions.quote: s. 503(1) (a) Cr. C. requires that a person who is arrested and detained be taken before a justice “without unreasonable delay” and in any event within 24 hours after the arrest.

propositions.text: Section 515 requires release unless prosecution shows cause for continued detention.
propositions.quote: Section 515 Cr. C. provides that the justice shall release the person unless the prosecution shows cause why the detention should be continued.

propositions.text: Prosecution has limited grounds and short time to justify detention, possibly insufficient to investigate fully.
propositions.quote: In the short time it has before it must show cause why the detention of the accused in custody is justified, the prosecution has to gather the evidence it intends to use at the bail hearing

propositions.text: Section 516(1) limits bail hearing adjournments to three days without accused's consent; orders can be reviewed with notice.
propositions.quote: Section 516(1) Cr. C. provides that the adjournment of a bail hearing cannot exceed three days except with the consent of the accused; and orders can be reviewed at the request of the accused provided that the accused has given the prosecution two days’ notice

paragraphs.summary: The court describes bail hearing rules requiring prompt hearings, limited prosecution time, and limited adjournments.

propositions.text: Compromises on evidence nature at bail hearings exist to avoid prejudicial delay.
propositions.quote: To avoid any delay prejudicial to an accused who ought to be released, while at the same time ensuring that those who do not meet the criteria for release are kept in custody, compromises had to be made regarding the nature of the evidence to be adduced at the bail hearing.

propositions.text: Prosecution may lead any credible or trustworthy evidence, including untested or hearsay evidence.
propositions.quote: According to s. 518(1)(e) Cr. C., the prosecutor may lead any evidence that is “credible or trustworthy”, which might include evidence of a confession that has not been tested for voluntariness or consistency with the Charter , bad character, information obtained by wiretap, hearsay statements, ambiguous post-offence conduct, untested similar facts, prior convictions, untried charges, or personal information on living and social habits.

propositions.text: Justice has broad discretion to inquire of accused; bail hearings are informal and can be by phone.
propositions.quote: The justice has a broad discretion to “make such inquiries, on oath or otherwise, of and concerning the accused as he considers desirable” (s. 518(1)(a)). The process is informal; the bail hearing can even take place over the phone (s. 515(2.2)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains bail hearings allow broad, informal evidence and inquiries to avoid delay.

propositions.text: Appellants argue the mandatory publication ban was not part of initial reform and not debated in Parliament.
propositions.quote: The appellants consider it significant that the mandatory publication ban was not part of the initial reform package and was not commented on during the debate in Parliament

propositions.text: Two points respond: Ouimet Report's recommendation and ban on publishing preliminary inquiry evidence.
propositions.quote: Two points have to be made with respect to this argument. The first is found in the Ouimet Report itself, and the second relates to the ban on publishing evidence taken at preliminary inquiries.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue ban was not initially included or debated; court notes Ouimet Report and preliminary inquiry ban respond to this.

propositions.text: Parliament followed most Ouimet Report recommendations, including mandatory ban if accused sought it.
propositions.quote: Parliament chose to follow most of the recommendations of the Ouimet Report. They had recommended that, if the accused sought a ban, it be mandatory.

propositions.text: Mandatory ban aimed to prevent prejudicing accused by dissemination of prejudicial, irrelevant, or inadmissible matter.
propositions.quote: The mandatory ban was seen as a measure “taken to prevent prejudicing the accused at his trial by the dissemination of prejudicial matter which would not be relevant or admissible at his trial”

propositions.text: Omission of ban from initial bill likely rectified by later inclusion; no argument from initial omission.
propositions.quote: it is safe to assume that the purpose of including it was to rectify this omission. Therefore, in my view, no argument can be drawn from the fact that the ban was not part of the initial version of the new bail provisions

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament adopted Ouimet's mandatory ban recommendation to prevent prejudicial dissemination, rectifying initial omission.

propositions.text: Mandatory publication bans existed, e.g. s. 539 Cr. C. for preliminary inquiry evidence.
propositions.quote: mandatory publication bans were not unknown at the time of the Ouimet Report. For instance, s. 539 Cr. C. requires that a ban on the publication of evidence adduced at a preliminary inquiry be ordered should the accused apply for one.

propositions.text: Standing Committee discussed preliminary inquiry ban; Minister Turner justified it to prevent prejudicial pre-trial publicity.
propositions.quote: Minister Turner justified it as follows: We are not talking about a situation of legitimate publicity at an open trial once the jury is empanelled...

propositions.text: Comments show goal beyond jury bias, addressing broader fair trial protection.
propositions.quote: These comments go beyond averting jury bias. They address the broader goal of protecting the right to a fair trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes existing mandatory bans on preliminary inquiry evidence aimed at protecting fair trial rights beyond jury bias.

propositions.text: Analogy between preliminary inquiry ban and bail hearing ban due to low evidentiary threshold and one-sided evidence risk.
propositions.quote: A direct, and helpful, analogy can be drawn between the ban at a preliminary inquiry and the one at a bail hearing...

propositions.text: In both proceedings, Crown must only make prima facie case; defence may not challenge evidence, risking one-sided publicity affecting trial fairness.
propositions.quote: The Crown need tender only enough evidence to make out a prima facie case, and the defence may for strategic reasons choose not to call witnesses or otherwise challenge the Crown’s evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds bail hearing and preliminary inquiry bans analogous due to low evidence threshold and risk of one-sided publicity.

propositions.text: A rational connection exists between bail reform components including the publication ban.
propositions.quote: a rational connection can clearly be found in the interplay between the various components of the reform.

propositions.text: Will next assess minimal impairment stage of Oakes test regarding ban's impact on free expression.
propositions.quote: This brings me to the third stage of the Oakes analysis, that of minimal impairment, which entails an assessment of the impact of the ban on free expression.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes a rational connection exists and proceeds to assess minimal impairment of the ban on free expression.

propositions.text: Bail hearings occur early in proceedings and attract media attention, especially in high-profile cases.
propositions.quote: the bail hearing is conducted at the very beginning of the criminal proceeding. Bail hearings often attract considerable media attention, especially in highly visible cases like the ones presently before this Court.

propositions.text: Nature of expression at bail hearings must be considered in assessing ban's impact.
propositions.quote: In assessing the impact of the ban, the court must consider the nature of the expression at issue

paragraphs.summary: The court notes bail hearings are early and media-attractive, so expression nature must be considered in impact assessment.

propositions.text: Minimal impairment must be assessed considering other measures to meet Parliament's objectives.
propositions.quote: To determine whether the limit impairs a right as little as possible, it must be assessed in light of the other measures adopted to meet Parliament’s objectives.

propositions.text: Rosenberg J.A. and Slatter J.A. noted publication ban hearings would burden accused and delay bail hearings.
propositions.quote: As pointed out by Rosenberg J.A. in the Ontario case (para. 38) and Slatter J.A. in the Alberta case (para. 36), if the justice were to hold a publication ban hearing, the accused would have to prepare for that hearing...

paragraphs.summary: The court states minimal impairment must consider other measures; prior judges noted ban hearings burden accused and delay bail.

propositions.text: Ouimet Report authors observed initial stage of process is crucial.
propositions.quote: The authors of the Ouimet Report observed that the initial stage of the process is crucial (pp. 101-2).

propositions.text: Publication ban hearings would burden vulnerable accused who may lack counsel and knowledge of prosecution evidence.
propositions.quote: If a publication ban hearing were to be held, an additional burden would be placed on the accused at a time when he or she is extremely vulnerable.

propositions.text: Alberta Court of Appeal found no justification for common law restriction due to resource burden.
propositions.quote: the Alberta Court of Appeal found it significant that neither the Crown nor Mr. White had attempted to justify a common law restriction in that court, to which the statutory mandatory ban does not apply; the court attributed this to the resources that would have to be expended

paragraphs.summary: The court finds publication ban hearings burden vulnerable accused; Alberta Court noted resource burden justified statutory ban.

propositions.text: Given delay, resources, and prejudice, no less impairing measure than the ban is imaginable.
propositions.quote: it would be difficult to imagine a measure capable of achieving Parliament’s objectives that would involve a more limited impairment of freedom of expression.

propositions.text: Adding unrelated issues to bail hearing would delay justice administration.
propositions.quote: If issues unrelated to the release of the accused were added to the bail hearing, this would require the consideration of matters extraneous to the bail process and could have a domino effect on other bail hearings

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no less impairing measure than the ban exists and adding issues would delay justice.

propositions.text: Section 517 ban prohibits publication of evidence and reasons at bail hearing, not identity or basic facts.
propositions.quote: The provision only prohibits the publication of evidence adduced, information given, representations made, and reasons given by the justice at a bail hearing. But the media can publish the identity of the accused, comment on the facts and the offence

propositions.text: Media can report legal conditions of release and outcome of bail application.
propositions.quote: Journalists are also not prevented from informing the public of the legal conditions attached to the release of the accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the ban limits publication of bail hearing evidence but allows reporting identity, facts, and bail outcomes.

propositions.text: Ban is temporary, ending after preliminary inquiry or trial, covering only bail process information.
propositions.quote: The temporary nature of the ban is another important factor. The ban ends when the accused is discharged after a preliminary inquiry, or at the end of the trial.

propositions.text: Information can be made public later when complete trial information is available.
propositions.quote: the information it covers can eventually be made public once more complete information produced in accordance with the standards applicable to criminal trials is available.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the ban is temporary and information can be published later with full trial information.

propositions.text: Ban does not impair freedom of expression more than necessary; it is limited, temporary, and covers untested, often irrelevant information.
propositions.quote: the ban cannot be said to impair freedom of expression more than is necessary. The ban is limited to a preliminary stage of the criminal justice process and is not absolute, and the information the media are prevented from publishing is untested, and is often one-sided and largely irrelevant to the search for truth.

propositions.text: Ban may make journalists' work harder but does not prevent conveying basic relevant information.
propositions.quote: The ban may make journalists’ work more difficult, but it does not prevent them from conveying and commenting on basic, relevant information.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the ban minimally impairs expression, covering untested info and allowing basic reporting despite some difficulty for journalists.

propositions.text: Alternatives to mandatory ban would be equally effective and less restrictive on freedom of expression
propositions.quote: The appellants suggest alternatives that would in their view be equally effective and trench less on freedom of expression.

propositions.text: Risk to fair trial can be addressed by later procedures like challenges for cause, venue changes, sequestration
propositions.quote: They submit that any risk to a fair trial can be addressed by means of procedures that arise later in the process, such as challenges for cause, changes of venue and sequestration.

propositions.text: Alternatives are unsatisfactory as they only address bias, not expeditious bail hearing or early release needs
propositions.quote: The alternatives put forward are unsatisfactory. All of them relate solely to the need to avert bias. They do not address the other considerations which favour a publication ban, namely the need to ensure an expeditious bail hearing and an early release of the accused.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue alternatives to mandatory ban suffice; court finds they only address bias, not expeditious bail or early release needs.

propositions.text: Suggest time-limited publication ban at bail hearing, lasting until hearing end, then merits hearing
propositions.quote: The appellants also suggest that a time-limited publication ban could be imposed at the outset of the bail hearing that would last only until the end of that hearing, at which time a hearing would be held on the merits of continuing the ban.

propositions.text: This suggestion is unacceptable as parties need to know at bail hearing if information will be published
propositions.quote: This suggestion is no more acceptable than the first. The parties need to know at the bail hearing if the information given there will be published.

propositions.text: Accused might alter bail approach or forego bail if they know info will be published next day
propositions.quote: Accused persons could alter their approaches to the bail hearing, or perhaps even forego requesting bail, if they know that everything they say could be in the newspaper the next morning.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants suggest time-limited ban; court rejects as parties must know publication status at bail hearing to avoid altered accused behavior.

propositions.text: Knowledge of possible publication forces accused to make premature, strategic decisions risking rights
propositions.quote: If they know that evidence could be published, accused persons might have to make decisions they would not otherwise have made at a time when they can only speculate on what the Crown intends to adduce at the bail hearing.

propositions.text: Canadian Newspapers Co. upheld mandatory ban on publishing complainant identity to ensure certainty
propositions.quote: In Canadian Newspapers Co. v. Canada (Attorney General), [1988] 2 S.C.R. 122, this Court upheld s. 442(3) Cr. C., which provided for a mandatory ban on publishing the identity of a complainant in a sexual assault case should the complainant apply for one.

propositions.text: Certainty of non-publication at reporting decision time is vital to encourage reporting sexual assault
propositions.quote: Obviously, since fear of publication is one of the factors that influences the reporting of sexual assault, certainty with respect to non-publication at the time of deciding whether to report plays a vital role in that decision.

propositions.text: Discretionary ban would defeat Parliament's objective by depriving victim of certainty
propositions.quote: Therefore, a discretionary provision under which the judge retains the power to decide whether to grant or refuse the ban on publication would be counterproductive, since it would deprive the victim of that certainty.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal accepted certainty argument for bail hearing publication ban
propositions.quote: In the Ontario case, the Ontario Court of Appeal accepted the certainty argument in the context of the bail hearing.

propositions.text: Without knowing if ban applies, accused cannot risk contesting bail due to jury bias risk
propositions.quote: Without knowing whether or not the publication ban will be in place, the accused cannot know whether to take the risk of contesting bail to possibly obtain the immediate reward of release at the cost of the more serious risk of poisoning the minds of jurors at the subsequent trial

propositions.text: Rejects suggestion to authorize publication at bail hearing and impose discretionary ban later
propositions.quote: On this same basis, I would reject the suggestion that the publication of information be authorized at the time of the bail hearing and that a discretionary ban then be imposed closer to the trial date.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds knowledge of publication risks forces accused to premature decisions; prior cases stress certainty of ban; rejects discretionary ban suggestion.

propositions.text: Publication ban hearing before or after bail hearing is not reasonable alternative to mandatory ban
propositions.quote: It follows that a publication ban hearing, whether held before or after the bail hearing, is not a reasonable alternative to a mandatory ban.

propositions.text: Accused would struggle to show ban necessary to prevent real and substantial trial fairness risk
propositions.quote: it would be difficult for the accused to discharge the burden of showing that the ban would be “necessary in order to prevent a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the trial”

propositions.text: Justice would have difficulty performing duties judicially under such circumstances
propositions.quote: Therefore, the justice would have difficulty performing his or her duties in a judicial manner.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds publication ban hearing not reasonable alternative; accused would struggle to prove necessity; justice would struggle to act judicially.

propositions.text: Discretionary ban solely on justice's reasons would not serve provision's objectives
propositions.quote: I am also of the opinion that to hold that the ban is discretionary solely with respect to the justice’s reasons would not serve the objectives of the provision.

propositions.text: Imposing constraints on justice to give expeditious, non-prejudicial reasons is unacceptable
propositions.quote: Even if it could be argued that the justice could expeditiously give reasons that would not unduly risk jury bias or otherwise feed dangerous pre‑trial publicity, to impose such constraints on the justice at this time would be unacceptable.

propositions.text: Such constraints invite parties to argue on ban and reasons content, consuming time and resources
propositions.quote: This would inevitably invite the parties to present arguments on the discretionary ban and on the content of the reasons likely to be published. Preparing arguments takes time and resources.

propositions.text: Crafting meaningful reasons without disclosing prejudicial untested evidence at early stage is complex
propositions.quote: one should not underestimate the complexity of crafting meaningful reasons without disclosing potentially determinative untested evidence at a stage at which neither the justice nor the accused can foresee what information will be prejudicial to the right of the accused to a fair trial.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds discretionary ban on justice's reasons unworkable due to complexity, resource demands, and risk of prejudicial disclosure.

propositions.text: Prosecutor's discretion to apply ban does not undermine legislation's objectives
propositions.quote: The fact that Parliament chose to make the ban discretionary where the prosecutor is the applicant does not undermine the legislation’s objectives.

propositions.text: Prosecutor better positioned than accused to meet Dagenais test due to knowledge and resources
propositions.quote: The prosecutor is in a better position than the accused to meet the Dagenais test. Unlike the accused, the prosecutor knows exactly what allegations are to be made against the accused and also knows what evidence will likely be introduced at trial.

propositions.text: Prosecutor has resources for counsel for publication ban and bail hearings unlike accused
propositions.quote: Moreover, the prosecutor does not face the problem of finding resources such as, most importantly, for counsel for both the publication ban and the bail hearings.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds prosecutor's discretion to apply ban aligns with objectives due to better knowledge and resources than accused.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal limited mandatory ban to cases where jury trial possible
propositions.quote: The majority of the Ontario Court of Appeal read the provision down in part, limiting the mandatory publication ban to cases in which a jury trial is possible.

propositions.text: Fair trial rights not at risk where judge alone exposed to prejudicial info
propositions.quote: They concluded that “[f]air trial rights cannot be said to be at risk where a judge, sitting alone, is exposed to prejudicial information which should not be admitted at trial”

propositions.text: Dissent would remove mandatory nature of ban
propositions.quote: The dissent would have read out the mandatory nature of the ban.

propositions.text: Majority's reading limited impact as accused usually hasn't elected trial mode at bail hearing
propositions.quote: the practical impact of the majority’s conclusion is limited, since at the time of the bail hearing, the accused has usually not yet made an election and not yet ruled out the possibility of being tried by a jury.

propositions.text: Small percentage of charges tried by jury is not determinative as bail hearing is early stage
propositions.quote: The fact that only a small percentage of criminal charges are actually heard by a jury is therefore not determinative.

propositions.text: Even if provision read down, ban applies in vast majority of cases at bail hearing
propositions.quote: Because the bail hearing is held at the beginning of the process, even if the provision is read down as the majority have done, the ban would still apply in the vast majority of cases.

propositions.text: Reading down provision is unacceptable alternative as it fails to address appellants' concerns and timing/resource issues
propositions.quote: Thus, this alternative cannot be accepted. Not only does it fail to respond to the appellants’ concerns, but it fails to settle the timing and resource issues that arise in respect of the proposed publication ban hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Ontario Court of Appeal limited ban to jury trials; court finds this limited and rejects it as alternative due to timing and resource issues.

propositions.text: Suggest discretionary ban limited to prejudicial evidence
propositions.quote: One last alternative was suggested: imposing a discretionary ban limited to prejudicial evidence.

propositions.text: Discretionary ban limited to prejudicial evidence has same difficulties as publication ban hearing
propositions.quote: this suggestion presents the same difficulties as those that any publication ban hearing would entail.

propositions.text: At early stage, time and resources should focus on trial fairness
propositions.quote: at this early stage of the procedure allocation of time and resources should focus on the fairness of the trial of the accused.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants suggest discretionary ban on prejudicial evidence; court finds it shares difficulties of ban hearing and distracts from trial fairness focus.

propositions.text: Mandatory publication ban integral to measures ensuring trial fairness and expeditious bail hearing
propositions.quote: I conclude that the mandatory publication ban is integral to a series of measures designed to foster trial fairness and ensure an expeditious bail hearing.

propositions.text: Ban meets minimal impairment stage of Oakes test
propositions.quote: It meets the requirements of the minimal impairment stage of the Oakes test.

propositions.text: Ban must also have benefits outweighing deleterious effects
propositions.quote: But this does not complete the analysis. The ban must also be found to have benefits that outweigh its deleterious effects.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes mandatory ban is integral and minimally impairing but must also have benefits outweighing harms.

propositions.text: Final Oakes stage focuses on consequences of impugned measure, not reiteration of prior stages
propositions.quote: As the Chief Justice stated in Hutterian Brethren (at para. 76), the final stage of the Oakes analysis is not a reiteration of the previous ones. Whereas the focus of the first three stages is on Parliament’s objective, the final stage concerns the consequences of the impugned measure.

paragraphs.summary: Final Oakes stage concerns consequences of measure, not reiteration of prior stages, per Chief Justice in Hutterian Brethren.

propositions.text: Mandatory ban limits accused's liberty deprivation by confining bail hearing issues to bail-related matters
propositions.quote: it limits the deprivation of the liberty of the accused by confining the issues at the bail hearing to those specifically related to bail.

propositions.text: First day in custody may be overwhelming, especially with unsatisfactory detention conditions
propositions.quote: The first day in custody may be overwhelming for an accused; this is especially true if the conditions of detention are unsatisfactory.

propositions.text: Liberty lost is never regained; justice system must minimize unwarranted liberty denial
propositions.quote: At the heart of a free and democratic society is the liberty of its subjects. Liberty lost is never regained and can never be fully compensated for; therefore, where the potential exists for the loss of freedom for even a day, we, as a free and democratic society, must place the highest emphasis on ensuring that our system of justice minimizes the chances of an unwarranted denial of liberty.

propositions.text: Ban ensures accused focus on liberty interests, not privacy, and protects public from untested stigmatizing info
propositions.quote: It ensures that they will not renounce their right to liberty in order to protect their reputations. It also ensures that the public will not be influenced by untested, one-sided and stigmatizing information bearing on issues that are often irrelevant to guilt.

propositions.text: Ban aligns with other Criminal Code publication bans like s. 539 on preliminary inquiry evidence
propositions.quote: It ensures consistency with the objectives of other publication bans provided for in the Criminal Code , such as the one under s. 539 concerning evidence produced at a preliminary inquiry.

paragraphs.summary: Mandatory ban limits liberty deprivation, helps accused focus on liberty, protects public from prejudicial info, and aligns with other bans.

propositions.text: Bail hearing info often concerns accused's character, not crime
propositions.quote: the information relevant to interim release often relates to the character of the individual accused and not to the crime

propositions.text: Evidence at bail hearing concerns accused's personality and risk, not guilt
propositions.quote: Evidence will bear not on whether the accused committed the crime, but on the accused as an individual: what kind of person he or she is, and whether he or she is likely to be a danger for society or to appear at trial.

propositions.text: Accused may denounce co-accused as 'bad guy' with untested evidence at bail hearing
propositions.quote: one accused might choose at the bail hearing to denounce a co-accused as the “bad guy” and to adduce additional untested evidence for that purpose

propositions.text: Mandatory ban limits pre-trial disclosure of inadmissible or unreliable info in conflicting accused cases
propositions.quote: In such circumstances, a mandatory ban limits the pre-trial disclosure of information that may be inadmissible at trial or highly unreliable.

paragraphs.summary: Bail hearing info often concerns character; mandatory ban limits pre-trial disclosure of unreliable or inadmissible info among conflicting accused.

propositions.text: Duty counsel conduct most Ontario bail hearings under difficult conditions and time constraints
propositions.quote: two experienced Crown counsel confirmed in affidavits that duty counsel conduct most bail hearings in Ontario; they often prepare for and conduct them under difficult circumstances.

propositions.text: Newly arrested accused often have limited understanding and ability to instruct counsel
propositions.quote: newly arrested accused persons often have only a limited understanding of the court system and the charges facing them, and a limited ability to instruct counsel

paragraphs.summary: Duty counsel conduct most Ontario bail hearings under difficult conditions; accused often have limited understanding and ability to instruct counsel.

propositions.text: Accused can apply for publication ban which must be ordered without discretion
propositions.quote: It is in this context that an accused can apply for a publication ban, and when such an application is made, the justice has no discretion. The ban must be ordered.

propositions.text: Ban applies to evidence, info, representations, and reasons at bail hearing until discharge or trial end
propositions.quote: It applies to the evidence taken, information given and representations made at the hearing, and to any reasons given for the order made under s. 515 . It remains in effect until the accused is discharged after a preliminary inquiry or until the end of the trial, as the case may be.

propositions.text: Much bail hearing evidence presumptively inadmissible at trial
propositions.quote: A large part of the evidence taken at the bail hearing is presumptively inadmissible at trial.

propositions.text: Information about accused often irrelevant to truth-seeking at trial
propositions.quote: such information is often irrelevant to the search for truth in relation to the offence, which is the actual purpose of the criminal trial.

paragraphs.summary: Accused can apply for mandatory ban covering bail hearing evidence and reasons, much of which is inadmissible and irrelevant to trial truth.

propositions.text: Discretionary ban would cause adjournments, longer hearings, and additional issues
propositions.quote: A discretionary ban would entail additional issues and adjournments, and would result in longer hearings.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal noted bail court backlog and systemic delay in bail system
propositions.quote: Feldman J.A., writing for the majority of the Ontario Court of Appeal in the Ontario case, mentioned a current problem in some overburdened Ontario bail courts (at paras. 198-99): in R. v. Jevons, 2008 ONCJ 559, [2008] O.J. No. 4397 (QL), De Filippis J. had described the backlog plaguing the bail courts and concluded that the accused in that case was the victim of systemic delay in the bail system and that his right to reasonable bail had been infringed.

propositions.text: Court must consider constraints when assessing consequences of process changes like publication ban hearing
propositions.quote: courts must be alert to those constraints when assessing the consequences of any change to a process, such as the inclusion of a publication ban hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Discretionary ban would cause delays; bail courts face backlogs; courts must consider constraints when assessing process changes.

propositions.text: In Ontario case, accused appeared multiple times quickly; bail hearings held June 12, ban ordered then
propositions.quote: The arrests were made on June 2, 2006. Between June 3 and June 12, each of the accused appeared in court at least once; for some of them, it was the third appearance. The bail hearings were held on June 12, 2006. The publication ban was then ordered, and it was to apply to all the accused.

propositions.text: Publication ban hearing would have delayed ban order due to notice and conflicting counsel positions
propositions.quote: In light of notice requirements and the conflicting positions taken by counsel for the various accused, this could not have been done as quickly had a publication ban hearing been held.

paragraphs.summary: Ontario case shows quick bail hearings and ban orders; publication ban hearing would have delayed ban due to notice and conflicts.

propositions.text: Bail hearings would rarely be delayed if ban discretionary as Dagenais test rarely met
propositions.quote: The appellants argue that bail hearings would almost never be delayed if the ban were discretionary because the Dagenais test would rarely be met, since jury bias is purely speculative.

propositions.text: Counsel would seldom bring motions for bans under discretionary regime
propositions.quote: As a result, counsel would seldom bring motions for bans.

propositions.text: Appellants wrongly assume accused would renounce trial fairness to ensure expeditious hearing
propositions.quote: This proposition is based on the assumption that accused would renounce their interest in trial fairness to ensure an expeditious hearing.

propositions.text: Mandatory ban intended to avoid accused compromising trial fairness for expediency
propositions.quote: This is exactly the kind of compromise the mandatory ban is intended to avoid.

propositions.text: Appellants incorrectly view ban as unrelated to accused's fair trial and bail rights
propositions.quote: The appellants’ argument is in fact based on the incorrect view that the ban has nothing to do with the rights of the accused to a fair trial and to fair access to bail.

propositions.text: Bail hearing and info disclosure affect accused's interests
propositions.quote: It is simply wrong to assume that neither the bail hearing itself nor the disclosure of information, evidence or the reasons for the justice’s order would have any effect on the accused’s interests.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue discretionary ban would rarely delay bail; court rejects, finding ban protects accused's fair trial and bail rights.

propositions.text: Ban limits media from informing public on matters of interest, impairing freedom of expression
propositions.quote: Section 517 Cr. C. bars the media from informing the population on matters of interest which could otherwise be subject more widely to public debate

propositions.text: Ban impairs freedom to discuss government institutions, policies, and practices
propositions.quote: it impairs “[t]he freedom of individuals to discuss information about the institutions of government, [and] their policies and practices”

paragraphs.summary: Court acknowledges ban limits media freedom to inform public and discuss government matters.

propositions.text: Ban prevents full public access and scrutiny of criminal justice process
propositions.quote: The ban prevents full public access to, and full scrutiny of, the criminal justice process.

propositions.text: Bail hearing may attract media attention but outcome may be misunderstood by public
propositions.quote: Moreover, the bail hearing may attract considerable media attention and its outcome may not be fully understood by the public

propositions.text: Media better equipped to explain judicial process if info not restricted
propositions.quote: In such cases, the media would be better equipped to explain the judicial process to the public if the information they could convey were not restricted.

paragraphs.summary: Ban limits public scrutiny; bail hearings attract media but public may misunderstand; media could better explain if info unrestricted.

propositions.text: Deleterious effects of ban outweighed by need for certainty, timeliness, resource conservation, and trial fairness
propositions.quote: on balance, I must find that in the context of the bail process, the deleterious effects of the limits on the publication of information are outweighed by the need to ensure certainty and timeliness, to conserve resources, and to avert the disclosure of untested prejudicial information; in other words, to guarantee as much as possible trial fairness and fair access to bail.

propositions.text: Mandatory ban is reasonable compromise despite imperfection
propositions.quote: Although not a perfect outcome, the mandatory ban represents a reasonable compromise.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes ban's harms are outweighed by benefits ensuring trial fairness and bail access; ban is reasonable compromise.

propositions.text: Does the publication ban apply to all the co-accused in the Ontario case?
propositions.quote: does the publication ban apply to all the co-accused?

propositions.text: The Criminal Code is silent on whether the publication ban applies to all co-accused, so common law jurisdiction applies.
propositions.quote: The Criminal Code is silent on this point, and a justice must resort to his or her common law jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Ontario courts correctly exercised jurisdiction and held the ban applies to all accused to be effective.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Ontario courts correctly exercised their jurisdiction in answering the question in the affirmative.

propositions.text: A publication ban is effective only if it applies to all accused because evidence against parties overlaps greatly.
propositions.quote: A publication ban will be effective only if it applies to all the accused. Clearly, the evidence against the parties will overlap to a great extent.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises whether the publication ban applies to all co-accused, finds the Criminal Code silent, and agrees Ontario courts correctly held the ban applies to all accused.

propositions.text: Appellants raise additional issues in Alberta case about jurisdiction, mootness, and functus officio.
propositions.quote: In the Alberta case, the appellants raise a number of additional issues based on jurisdiction, mootness and functus officio.

propositions.text: Appellants mention Court of Appeal's criticism of raising constitutional challenge in criminal proceeding rather than civil action.
propositions.quote: They also mention the Court of Appeal’s criticism of the choice to raise the constitutional challenge in the context of a criminal proceeding rather than by bringing a civil action.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants in Alberta case raise issues on jurisdiction, mootness, functus officio, and Court of Appeal's criticism of constitutional challenge method.

propositions.text: Appellants acknowledge Supreme Court need not rule on additional issues as it has jurisdiction over appeal substance.
propositions.quote: the appellants expressly acknowledge that this Court does not need to rule on them, because it has jurisdiction to entertain the substance of the appeal in any event.

propositions.text: It is unnecessary to deal with the additional issues raised by appellants.
propositions.quote: It is therefore not necessary to deal with them.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants acknowledge Court need not rule on additional issues; court finds it unnecessary to address them.

propositions.text: Section 517 infringes freedom of expression but is demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
propositions.quote: s. 517 Cr. C. infringes freedom of expression but that the limit can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

propositions.text: Appellants sought to strike down the mandatory wording of section 517.
propositions.quote: Since the appellants sought to strike down the mandatory wording of the provision,

propositions.text: The appeals are dismissed, constitutionality of section 517 upheld, and cross-appeal in Ontario case allowed.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss their appeals. I would uphold the constitutionality of the provision and allow the cross-appeal in the Ontario case.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes section 517 infringes expression but is justified; dismisses appeals, upholds constitutionality, allows Ontario cross-appeal.

propositions.text: Abella J. dissenting emphasizes the open court principle protecting public's right to know court proceedings.
propositions.quote: This Court has a long pedigree in protecting the public’s right to be aware of what takes place in the country’s courtrooms.

propositions.text: Open court principle requires public access to judicial process to maintain trust and enable meaningful discussion.
propositions.quote: to maintain public trust in the justice system, the public must be able to see the judicial process at work.

propositions.text: Edmonton Journal v. Alberta affirms public's right to information about courts to assess institutions and discuss proceedings.
propositions.quote: members of the public have a right to information pertaining to public institutions and particularly the courts. . . . Only then can they make an assessment of the institution.

propositions.text: Public discussion and criticism depend on media providing information about court proceedings.
propositions.quote: Discussion of court cases and constructive criticism of court proceedings is dependent upon the receipt by the public of information as to what transpired in court.

paragraphs.summary: Abella J. dissent stresses open court principle and cites Edmonton Journal affirming public's right to court information for trust and discussion.

propositions.text: Whether a mandatory publication ban on bail hearing information is justified or should be discretionary based on fair trial interests.
propositions.quote: The issue in this case is whether a ban on bail hearing information should be mandatory ... or only imposed when the accused demonstrates fair trial interests demand it.

propositions.text: Abella J. agrees with Rosenberg J.A. that mandatory ban in section 517 fails final Oakes test stage.
propositions.quote: I am of the view ... that the mandatory ban in s. 517 ... does not survive the final stage of the Oakes test.

propositions.text: Appropriate remedy is to sever mandatory aspect of section 517 and leave discretion to order ban per Dagenais and Mentuck.
propositions.quote: the appropriate remedy is to sever the mandatory aspect of s. 517 and leave in place the discretion to order a ban, to be exercised in accordance with Dagenais ... and Mentuck.

paragraphs.summary: Abella J. finds mandatory ban unjustified, agrees with Rosenberg J.A., and proposes severing mandatory ban to allow discretionary orders.

propositions.text: Section 517 automatically prohibits disclosure of bail hearing reasons and information upon accused's request.
propositions.quote: Section 517 of the Criminal Code automatically prevents disclosure of the judge’s reasons and of any information at a bail hearing whenever the accused requests a ban.

propositions.text: Public and press can attend bail hearing but dissemination of information is mandatorily prohibited until trial completion.
propositions.quote: Neither the public nor the press is prevented from actually being in court during the hearing, but what is mandatorily prohibited is the public dissemination of what is disclosed there until the trial is complete.

propositions.text: This prohibition denies most people access to key criminal justice information, interfering with open court principle.
propositions.quote: This has the effect, for all but the handful of people who are present in the courtroom, of denying access to information ... This denial is a profound interference with the open court principle.

paragraphs.summary: Section 517 bans public dissemination of bail hearing info upon accused's request, denying public access and infringing open court principle.

propositions.text: Rosenberg J.A. summarized that section 517 cuts off meaningful public debate on bail decisions when most needed.
propositions.quote: Section 517 cuts off meaningful and informed public debate about a fundamental aspect of the administration of criminal justice, the bail system, at the very time that the debate may be most important — when the decision is made to grant or deny bail.

propositions.text: Section 517 hinders debate on cases of public interest where accused on bail commits further crimes, leaving public to speculate.
propositions.quote: It also hinders debate in other circumstances of great public interest, as where an accused on bail commits another, perhaps serious crime. The public is left to speculate about why the accused was released ...

paragraphs.summary: Rosenberg J.A. found section 517 blocks public debate on bail decisions and hinders responses in high public interest cases.

propositions.text: R. v. Hall stresses public confidence requires justice to be seen to be done, especially in bail system.
propositions.quote: Where justice is not seen to be done by the public, confidence in the bail system and, more generally, the entire justice system may falter.

propositions.text: This principle underlies consideration of whether mandatory ban in section 517 is justified.
propositions.quote: This brings us to whether this harm is outweighed by the benefits of a mandatory ban.

paragraphs.summary: R. v. Hall emphasizes justice must be seen done for public confidence; court considers if mandatory ban's harm is outweighed by benefits.

propositions.text: Major benefits of mandatory ban are reduction in pre-trial publicity and delay.
propositions.quote: The major benefits attributed to the ban are the reduction in pre-trial publicity and delay.

propositions.text: These concerns can largely be attenuated and do not seriously infringe fair trial rights.
propositions.quote: Each of these concerns, in my view, can largely be attenuated, and neither represents a sufficiently serious infringement of fair trial rights.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds ban's benefits of reducing pre-trial publicity and delay can be mitigated and do not seriously infringe fair trial rights.

propositions.text: Dagenais and Mentuck require bans only when necessary to protect real and serious risks to fair trial or justice administration.
propositions.quote: bans were only to be imposed where they are “necessary” to protect against “real and substantial” risks to an accused’s fair trial rights ... or “serious” risks to the administration of justice

propositions.text: Section 517's automatic ban collapses constitutional framework by ignoring public's presumptive right to know courtroom events.
propositions.quote: Section 517 ... completely collapses the constitutional framework in Dagenais/Mentuck, leaving out of the balance entirely the public’s presumptive right to know what goes on in a courtroom.

paragraphs.summary: Dagenais/Mentuck require necessity for bans; section 517's automatic ban ignores public's right to know, collapsing constitutional balance.

propositions.text: Even if pre-trial publicity concerns are speculative, remedies like partial bans, challenges, or venue changes exist.
propositions.quote: there remains the possibility of remedies such as a partial ban, challenges for cause, or a change of venue if there is a sufficient risk of prejudice.

propositions.text: Properly instructed juries can disregard irrelevant evidence, supporting reliance on jury safeguards.
propositions.quote: We should also be able to rely on the ability of a properly instructed jury to disregard irrelevant evidence, a reliance that is at the foundation of our belief in juries in criminal trials

propositions.text: Berger J.A. observed in related Alberta case that jurors likely forget brief news clips before trial, with safeguards ensuring impartiality.
propositions.quote: I very much doubt that prospective jurors would retain and recall the details of a 30 second news clip ... the usual admonitions ... are ... sufficient safeguards to ensure that an impartial jury ... will be empanelled.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes remedies exist for publicity concerns and juries can disregard irrelevant evidence; Berger J.A. supports safeguards' effectiveness.

propositions.text: Section 517 only protects bail hearing info; no protection exists for prejudicial info from other sources.
propositions.quote: s. 517 only protects an accused from disclosure of pre-trial information from a bail hearing. There is no legislative protection from potentially prejudicial pre-trial information that emanates from sources other than the bail hearing.

propositions.text: Ban on bail hearing info alone is too porous to justify serious infringement of open court principle.
propositions.quote: In the absence of such a generalized ban, the benefit of a ban only on bail hearing information seems to me to be too porous to justify the seriousness of the infringement.

paragraphs.summary: Section 517 protects only bail hearing info; this limited ban is too porous to justify serious infringement of open court principle.

propositions.text: Reduction in delay is a benefit only if discretionary ban requests substantially elongate hearings.
propositions.quote: This is a concern only if one assumes that the request for a discretionary ban will substantially elongate the hearing.

propositions.text: It is unlikely that evidence would routinely cause protracted bail proceedings or that media notice is required in every case.
propositions.quote: It is hard for me to see what evidence would routinely result in a protracted bail proceeding. ... I make no such assumption.

propositions.text: Decision to give media notice is discretionary and not expected in every bail hearing ban request.
propositions.quote: While the decision to give notice is a matter of discretion for the judge ... it seems ... unrealistic to expect that submissions be invited from the media in every case where a publication ban ... is requested.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds delay reduction benefit depends on assumptions about hearing length and media notice, which are unlikely or discretionary.

propositions.text: Without automatic notice, most cases will have no undue delay from discretionary ban requests.
propositions.quote: In the absence of such automatic notice, there will be, in the overwhelming number of cases, no undue delay.

propositions.text: High-profile cases likely to contest bans are few; universal mandatory ban should not be judged on these cases.
propositions.quote: Those cases where the media is most likely to contest a ban are those few which have a higher profile. But I would not judge the desirability of a universal mandatory ban based on its effectiveness for a small percentage of cases.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds most cases will not have delay without automatic notice; universal mandatory ban should not be based on few high-profile cases.

propositions.text: Public confidence requires timely delivery of relevant information about justice system.
propositions.quote: Public confidence in the justice system requires relevant information delivered in a timely way.

propositions.text: Mandatory ban on bail application evidence and reasons restricts information when public interest is highest.
propositions.quote: A mandatory ban on the evidence heard and the reasons given in a bail application is a ban on the information when it is of most concern and interest to the public.

propositions.text: Restrictions on release of such information are justified only if benefits outweigh detrimental impact.
propositions.quote: Restrictions on the release of such information are only justified if their benefits outweigh their detrimental impact.

paragraphs.summary: Court states public confidence needs timely info; mandatory ban restricts info at critical time; restrictions justified only if benefits outweigh harm.

propositions.text: Benefits of section 517 ban are not proportional to harmful effects on open court principle.
propositions.quote: Given that the salutary effects of the ban under s. 517 are not proportional to the harmful effects flowing from the infringement of the open court principle,

propositions.text: Appeal allowed in Ontario and Alberta cases; mandatory ban words in section 517 struck out.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal in both the Ontario and Alberta cases and strike out the words in s. 517 that render the ban mandatory.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes ban's benefits do not outweigh harm; allows appeals and strikes mandatory ban wording in section 517.
